extracted.intended_audience: policy makers, agency officials, civil rights advocates, and legal practitioners involved in Title VI enforcement
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and procedural standards for filing, assessing jurisdictional sufficiency, investigating, coordinating, and resolving federal Title VI (race/color/national origin) complaints across multiple federal agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA jurisdictional sufficiency criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing Title VI complaints for jurisdictional sufficiency, EPA evaluates each complaint for compliance with four criteria:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the complaint describes the acts that allegedly violate EPA's Title VI regulations; whether the complaint identifies an EPA funding recipient as the respondent; whether the complaint is in writing; whether the complaint is filed within 180 calendar days of an alleged discriminatory activity. If any criteria are absent, EPA may request supplemental information; a complaint is not rejected on jurisdictional grounds until all efforts to identify information to satisfy the four criteria have been exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effort to obtain supplemental information before rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may contact the complainant to request supplemental information or clarification and may use internal resources to ascertain whether the complaint involves a recipient of federal financial assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact can be telephonic, electronic, written, or in person; EPA may communicate several times to obtain sufficient information. EPA states it will not reject on jurisdictional grounds until all efforts to identify necessary information have been exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold requirements for agency responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies maintain responsibility for investigating and resolving Title VI complaints that meet threshold requirements such as standing, timeliness, and ripeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These threshold factors determine whether an agency will accept and investigate a complaint; they are applied across agencies (EPA, DOT, etc.) when asserting jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive jurisdiction when agency is sole funder or within enforcement authority
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency maintains exclusive jurisdiction over Title VI complaints when permit recipients obtained federal funding solely from that agency or the complaints are clearly within the agency's enforcement authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When other agencies provided funding or share authority, responsibility may be coordinated or referred; exclusive jurisdiction affects who investigates and which remedies are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral and interagency coordination procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: When another federal agency has jurisdiction over a complaint originally filed with an agency, the complaint will be referred to that agency and written confirmation will be sent to the complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After referral, the originating agency remains involved to coordinate efforts and determine whether it or the other agency will be the lead investigator. If the receiving agency is lead, its actions have the same effect as measures the originating agency would have taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must cooperatively ensure compliance when multiple funders exist
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department of Justice instructs that when numerous recipients receive funding for similar purposes from two or more federal agencies, the agencies must cooperatively ensure compliance with Title VI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may proceed with coordinated investigations or independently investigate; when jointly investigated, agencies should inform complainants in writing that the matter is being jointly investigated and resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal, reconsideration, and notification practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Many agencies (EPA, DOT, etc.) do not have formal appeal processes; agencies may reconsider complaints and will notify complainants in writing of status or of referrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA: OCR may reconsider a complaint and will notify complainant in writing. DOT and others similarly lack formal appeal rights but may allow reconsideration on a case-by-case basis. Notification practices vary and some regulations do not require notifying complainants of enforcement attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing timeliness requirement (180 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Title VI complaints must generally be filed within 180 days of the alleged discriminatory activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 180-day deadline is repeatedly cited across agencies (EPA, DOT, DOI, HUD); some agencies (e.g., DOT) allow extensions by the Secretary. Missing timeliness may affect jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of legislative or appropriations riders on complaint processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative rider provisions can hold complaints in abeyance and create backlogs, significantly reducing the number of complaints an agency can investigate and resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: EPA had 64 complaints held in abeyance due to an appropriations rider (filed Oct 21, 1998–2001), demonstrating that budgetary or legislative constraints can delay determinations that should be made within regulatory deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource and staffing adequacy affects program effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's staffing and budgetary resources are critical factors in its ability to investigate and resolve Title VI complaints appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report cites OCR staffing and budget levels (e.g., OCR had 30.5 FTEs in Feb 2002; fully staffed would be 42.5 FTEs; task force staffing and $1.5M for contract assistance). Agencies compensate with staff details and inter-office assistance; insufficient staffing was a concern when task force became operational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive compliance reviews reduce complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine and comprehensive reviews of recipients' programs before complaints are filed would likely result in fewer Title VI complaints and swifter enforcement when complaints are filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: None of the reviewed agencies reported having regular, comprehensive compliance review programs; absence of formal compliance review programs impedes enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOT-specific filing and investigation timing provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: DOT requires complaints to be filed within 180 days unless an extension is granted by the Secretary; DOT regulations reference a 'prompt' investigation but do not set a specific timeline for initiating or concluding investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOT forwards accepted complaints to the appropriate operating administration; lack of specific timelines means investigations can take multiple years (examples given of complaints pending more than three years).

rubrics_metrics.name: DOT investigative and enforcement procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: DOT uses multidisciplinary teams for complex complaints and forwards investigations to relevant operating administrations; if a violation is found DOT attempts voluntary compliance, then follows regulatory procedures (notice of opportunity for hearing, administrative enforcement hearing, or referral to DOJ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If voluntary compliance fails, DOT may consider terminating or suspending federal financial assistance; DOT has authority to refer unresolved cases to DOJ or hold administrative hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOT jurisdictional thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: When DOT maintains exclusive jurisdiction, complaints must satisfy threshold requirements of recipient status, standing, statute of limitations, and ripeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOT shares responsibility with other agencies when multiple enforcement authorities are involved, particularly for safety-related matters; coordination with other agencies (e.g., HUD) is common.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOI filing and intake procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: DOI requires written complaints to be filed with the Secretary no later than 180 days from the date of alleged discrimination; bureau and office equal opportunity officers are responsible for investigating and processing complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOI's departmental Office for Equal Opportunity conducts investigations; in complex cases OEO assumes jurisdiction; DOI accepts complaints for investigation if jurisdictional elements (standing, DOI funding recipient involvement) are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOI lead-agency determination rule
rubrics_metrics.description: DOI accepts lead responsibility for investigating a jointly funded matter only if DOI provided the greatest amount of federal financial assistance or if the complaint involves a DOI mission-related program area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the funding recipient named in the complaint did not receive DOI funding, DOI refers the complaint to the appropriate federal agency and should inform parties when closing due to lack of jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOI requirement for recipients to maintain compliance reports (but lack of guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: DOI requires its funding recipients to maintain Title VI compliance reports of their activities and submit them to the Secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOI regulations neither provide guidance on how often compliance reports should be prepared nor specify under what circumstances these reports will be used to determine compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: HUD investigation structure and joint processing
rubrics_metrics.description: HUD's Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity (FHEO) is the sole operating administration responsible for investigating and resolving HUD Title VI complaints; HUD convenes compliance review teams for on-site reviews and often processes Title VI complaints jointly with other federal agencies or under the Fair Housing Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance review teams include FHEO staff and HUD program technical experts; joint investigations with EPA, DoD, etc., are common when multiple agencies have interest or authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: HUD enforcement steps to revoke or suspend funding
rubrics_metrics.description: To revoke or suspend funding for Title VI violations HUD must: advise the funding recipient of noncompliance; determine that compliance cannot be obtained voluntarily; have the HUD Secretary approve the action and file a full report with the appropriate congressional committee explaining the reasons for the proposed revocation or termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process is described as cumbersome and may deter use of revocation as an enforcement tool; HUD reported no instances of having withheld or revoked funding for Title VI violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification to complainants and recipients
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies vary in their notification practices; some regulations govern notifying recipients of violations but do not require notifying complainants of enforcement actions or attempts at voluntary compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: HUD's regulation governing notification to the recipient does not speak to notifying the complainant; DOT regulations do not establish a timeline for how long the agency has to conclude an investigation or for informing complainants of voluntary compliance attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-driven monitoring of complaint disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracking and reporting complaint intake and disposition (e.g., counts of rejected, dismissed, accepted, suspended, under review, partially dismissed, informally resolved, referred) is used to assess agency handling of Title VI complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: EPA reported 136 total complaints as of June 20, 2003, with 75 rejected; permitting-related complaints had high rejection rates. Such data highlight backlog, rejection rates, and potential systemic issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of task forces and inter-office resources to address backlog
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies can form task forces and reallocate staff across offices (detail assignments) and use contract assistance to handle backlogs and older complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: EPA's Title VI Task Force composed of personnel from enforcement, general counsel, regional counsel, solid waste, water, and civil rights; task force allocated $1.5 million for contract assistance and used staff detailed from other offices.
